📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Industry observers note that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that an AI coding agent rebuilt my photo-collage app as a distributed system and deployed it to a free server. The hard part turned out to be hardware: one free ARM CPU, 538 collages created during load testing, zero failed jobs, and $0 a month.

Like most developers, I have never been short of product ideas. Hosting them has always been the problem. I have tried shared hosting with SmartWeb, Azure free credits, Google Compute Engine’s free VM instances, SmartWeb’s virtual private servers, and Heroku dynos. None of them left me satisfied. The worst experience was a $200 charge for an AI address API on Google Cloud—for an application that never earned me a single kobo.

I am not a cheapskate, but I learned promptly that one of the easiest ways to kill a potentially good idea is to get the finances wrong. An application has to stay online until it reaches a critical mass of users, and hosting an untested, unverified product on expensive hardware can be wasteful.

Agentic AI coding has changed how quickly I can move from idea to production. Over about five weeks of intermittent coding—amounting to roughly three days of full work with Claude—my photo-stitching app went from an Angular 8 project that would not even build to a distributed system running in production.

According to recent reports, along the way, Claude upgraded the front end from Angular 8 to Angular 22 and fixed the build on Node 24. It set up RabbitMQ with Docker Compose so the message broker configures itself on startup, and added real-time notifications over SignalR with a progress spinner. It fixed a crash loop caused by an unreadable iPhone photo. It redesigned the system so any server can process any job, with switchable database and file storage, direct browser-to-storage uploads, and photos resized in the browser before upload. It added reliability work that a team might debate for a sprint: a dead-letter queue, confirmed publishing, idempotent workers, recovery of stuck jobs, and automatic clean-up. It fixed the stitching so photos keep their proportions and borders are even. It wrote 41 automated tests and scrubbed leaked passwords and personal photos from the Git history.

According to recent reports, coding, QA, DevOps, and production support used to be separate phases, often handled by separate people. Here they happened in one conversation. When code becomes this cheap to produce, the bottleneck moves. For me, it moved to hardware.

Bottleneck one: the machine on your desk.

To check what the AI builds, you have to run it locally. A distributed app means running the whole system locally: a web app, a background worker, a message broker, a database, and storage emulators. Because Claude adds features swiftly, and each one can add another container, it is easy to exhaust a laptop’s RAM and CPU.

According to recent reports, my setup made this lesson concrete. I work on a MacBook Air, with Visual Studio in a Windows virtual machine. Docker cannot run inside that VM on Apple Silicon, so Claude ran Docker on the Mac and drove it from Windows over SSH. Later, my mobile connection started dropping large packets and broke uploads from the VM, so Claude moved the load testing onto the server itself. The software problems took minutes. The hardware and network problems took longer.

Then comes hosting. Heroku looked like the easy route, but it has had no free dynos since 2022. The cheapest option is an Eco dyno at about $5 a month, plus about $5 for Postgres. That is affordable, but running it for an idea that has no users yet did not seem prudent.

Industry observers note that claude suggested Oracle Cloud’s Always Free tier: an ARM server with up to 4 CPUs and 24 GB of RAM, free with no end date. I created a small instance with 1 CPU and about 6 GB. Claude wrote a production Docker Compose file and a one-command setup script: Caddy as the gateway, the web app, the stitching worker, RabbitMQ, and PostgreSQL, with data that survives restarts. My repository is private, so rather than put a GitHub token on a public server, it copied the code over SSH and deployed it. The last blocker was mine to fix: opening ports 80 and 443 in Oracle’s network firewall. Then the site was live.

According to recent reports, I did not want to guess, so I asked Claude to load-test the live server. Simulated consumers ran the full flow: upload two photos, wait for the real-time notification, and download the stitched collage.

The server handled 64 people creating collages at the same moment without a single failed job: 538 collages, zero errors. Its ceiling was about 62 collages a minute—one per second. Beyond that, users queue. With 4 people creating at once, 95% of collages arrived within about five seconds; at 64, each person waited about a minute. If each active user makes a collage every couple of minutes, one CPU comfortably serves around 85 people at once, and a few hundred if they use it less often.

The test also revealed what runs out first, and it is not the CPU. Each collage stores about 5 MB, mostly the PNG output, so at full speed the disk would fill in under two hours. Switching to JPEG and shortening retention fixes that, and when traffic grows, three more free CPUs are waiting. That is the value of measuring before paying: I know what to change, and when.

Sources indicate that oracle isn’t being charitable. Servers need applications to run—ideally ones that go viral—and the free tier is a play for loyalty. Oracle wants successful projects to stay and grow into its paid services instead of moving off the platform once they reach critical mass. It can also reclaim free instances that sit idle.

Sources indicate that I think the bet is smart, and it points to a bigger trend. AI-generated code still needs energy to run and hardware to host it, even when far fewer people work on each project. As more people turn ideas into working software, demand for compute will keep growing, and I expect hosting and data centres to become a very profitable business.

For now, the combination works: Claude orchestrates the coding, QA, and DevOps, and Oracle’s free server keeps an idea online long enough to find out whether it deserves to grow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Burger King has confirmed a new collaboration with Peanuts, bringing Snoopy, Charlie Brown, and the rest of the gang to its restaurants for the holiday season with limited-time meals and exclusive collectibles.

Industry observers note that the fast food chain revealed the partnership on November 19, confirming that the holiday menu will launch at participating US locations on December 1, 2026. The promotion includes new food items, collectible packaging, and special merchandise for both adults and children.

The collaboration comes as Peanuts celebrates more than 75 years since its debut in 1950, with Burger King introducing two different meal options inspired by the franchise’s characters.

The main offering is the Peanuts Pack, which comes inside a collectible Snoopy Doghouse Box and includes one of two exclusive Snoopy holiday beanies.

Customers can choose between a Whopper with Cheese or 10-piece Chicken Nuggets, with the latter served alongside a new Woodstock Golden Ranch dipping sauce.

The meal also introduces Charlie Brown Loaded Potato Tots, featuring crispy, coin-shaped potatoes filled with cheese, bacon bits, sour cream, and chives.

Recent findings suggest that each Peanuts Pack comes with one of two collectible Snoopy beanies. One features a brown knit design with Snoopy resting on his red doghouse, while the other is red and depicts Snoopy wearing a Santa hat.

Sources indicate that burger King is also introducing a Peanuts-inspired King Jr. Meal, which includes a hamburger, cheeseburger, or four-piece Chicken Nuggets, alongside a choice of fries or applesauce and milk or apple juice.

Each kids’ meal comes in its own Snoopy Doghouse Box and includes one of eight collectible Peanuts toys.

Burger King debuts Hello Kitty kids meals with rare golden collectible toys.

Burger King unveils bizarre new burger with popcorn as a topping.

Burger King is releasing a Chocolate Whopper packed with dessert toppings.

The collection features Charlie Brown, Lucy, Linus, Sally, three different holiday-themed Snoopy figures, and a Snoopy Doghouse that comes with stickers for customization.

“Peanuts has been part of holiday family traditions for generations, and we can’t wait to bring Snoopy and the gang to Burger King this holiday season!” said Joel Yashinsky, Chief Marketing Officer of Burger King US and Canada.

“At BK, we go all out on partnerships to create fun experiences for everyone – with new menu items, creative packaging and crowns, collectible Snoopy beanies and Peanuts toys and more, we’ve created something really special. It’s holiday fun for all, and we can’t wait to welcome families and fans to BK to celebrate throughout the month of December!”.

Both meals will be available beginning December 1 at participating Burger King restaurants across the US, through the tech giant’s website, and via its mobile app while supplies last.

Burger King has not declared pricing for either meal or specified when the promotion will end.

The Peanuts collaboration isn’t the only holiday-themed fast food promotion arriving in December.

McDonald’s has also confirmed a limited-time Home Alone Meal launching December 1, featuring Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries and collectible socks inspired by the holiday movie. The promotion also brings Macaulay Culkin back as Kevin McCallister as part of the chain’s seasonal campaign.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KFC has unveiled a bizarre fresh fried cheese snack that looks ordinary on the outside, but reveals four different colors of melted cheese when pulled apart.

The fast food giant is no stranger to unusual menu creations, but its latest offering in Malaysia might be one of its most colorful yet.

Called Colourful Cheezy Cheese, the fresh item launched on November 18, 2026, featuring a crispy, golden-brown exterior packed with stretchy, multicolored cheese.

According to local promotional listings, Colourful Cheezy Cheese is available at participating KFC restaurants across Malaysia for RM7.49, equivalent to approximately $1.80 USD.

The snack resembles a large, breaded mozzarella stick flattened into a patty. However, pulling it apart reveals four different colors of gooey cheese rather than the usual white or yellow filling.

Despite the unusual appearance, KFC hasn’t publicly detailed how the different colors are achieved or whether they have distinct flavors.

The product is also being offered as part of KFC Malaysia’s new Holiday Bucket meals, with six-piece and ten-piece chicken bundles including one or two colorful cheese patties, respectively.

It’s another unusual creation from KFC’s international restaurants, which have been experimenting with increasingly outrageous menu items throughout 2026.

In August, KFC China left the chain’s main social media account baffled after unveiling a fried chicken burger featuring Oreo-flavored buns and sweet dipping sauces.

More recently, KFC South Korea introduced a massive Doom Triple Down sandwich as part of its Avengers: Doomsday collaboration, stacking three pieces of fried chicken together without a traditional bun.

For now, Colourful Cheezy Cheese is exclusive to Malaysia, with no announced plans to bring the rainbow-colored snack to restaurants in the United States or other markets.

KFC has also yet to confirm how long the colorful fried cheese will remain available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KFC Spain is celebrating the launch of GTA 6 with an unusual giveaway, offering fans a fried chicken disc to replace the missing physical disc in their game cases.

The promotion, called “The Replacement Disc,” comes as Rockstar’s highly anticipated game launched on November 19, 2026, following more than a decade of anticipation.

Unlike previous entries in the franchise, the physical edition includes a digital download code rather than a traditional game disc.

To mark the occasion, KFC has created a limited-edition fried chicken disc that fans can claim for free at select restaurants across Spain. The giveaway also includes special packaging designed to resemble a traditional video game case.

The Replacement Disc promotion runs on November 19 and 20 at ten participating KFC restaurants across Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Zaragoza, and Málaga.

According to recent reports, fans looking to claim one must bring their original GTA 6 game case to a participating location between 4 PM and 8 PM local time. Those who present their case will receive a free fried chicken disc while supplies last.

KFC has also designed exclusive packaging featuring Colonel Sanders on the cover, making it resemble a video game of its own.

The promotion is intended to recreate the experience of opening a physical game case and finding a disc inside, something that has become less common as publishers increasingly move toward digital distribution.

According to KFC Spain, the initiative was created in response to the ongoing shift away from physical media, particularly as collectors and players continue to debate the future of boxed video games.

Rather than offering a traditional replacement, the fast-food chain is giving fans an edible version that fits the theme of the launch.

KFC brings GTA-inspired Cluck n’ Bell to life with delivery car straight out of GTA 6.

KFC is hosting a fake funeral so GTA 6 fans can take the day off.

Kick and Twitch are giving away thousands of GTA 6 codes to viewers before launch.

In a recent development, this isn’t the only GTA 6 promotion KFC has launched. In Australia, the fast-food chain hosted a fake funeral for a fictional woman named “Ann Alibi”, giving fans an excuse to take time off work for the game’s release.

Building a Human Review Pipeline for AI Search: A Practical Developer’s Guide

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, weekly.
  • Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.

Imagine a documentation assistant answering a question about an API's current authentication requirements. It retrieves an outdated page, summarizes it fluently, and displays a citation. Every technical component appears to work, but the user receives instructions that no longer apply.

Automated checks are valuable, yet they cannot replace a clearly defined judgment about whether an answer solves the user's problem.

In a recent development, this guide builds a human-review workflow for a hypothetical API documentation assistant. You will define a review rubric, validate submissions with Python, measure reviewer disagreement, and turn accepted judgments into regression cases. The Python examples use Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn; they do not require a model-provider API key.

Start by identifying the failure you want to detect.

A documentation assistant usually has several stages: receive a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and present that answer with supporting material.

Do not collapse these into a single “good answer” rating. A low score without a reason tells the team little about what to fix.

SitePoint’s introduction to retrieval-augmented generation provides background on how retrieval and generation fit together.

Industry observers note that preserve the exact question, answer revision, retrieved passages, document versions, and retrieval timestamp for each run. Store a snapshot manifest with stable passage IDs, source URLs, and content hashes. Reviewers should see the material supplied to that run, not today’s edited page. Keep the model and prompt configuration with the run so a later review can be traced to the behavior it evaluated.

Sources indicate that A useful rubric defines observable criteria and separates evidence support from task completion and source suitability. Give each review the same user task and expected API version. Otherwise, reviewers may judge different questions while appearing to disagree about one answer.

For an answer about API authentication, use separate labels such as:.

Supported: every material factual claim is backed by the supplied evidence.

Partially supported: some material claims lack support, while others are grounded.

Unsupported: the answer's central instruction lacks support or contradicts the evidence.

Cannot assess: the necessary evidence is missing, unreadable, or inaccessible.

Recent findings suggest that define task completion independently as complete, incomplete, or cannot assess. For source suitability, use suitable, outdated, or cannot assess. An answer can faithfully summarize an obsolete page while failing the request for current instructions.

Sources indicate that consider a fictional API migration: version 2 accepts X-API-Key, while version 3 requires Authorization: Bearer . If the supplied evidence contains only the version 2 page, an answer repeating X-API-Key can be supported by its evidence but still use an outdated source. If the evidence explicitly requires Bearer and the answer invents X-API-Key, label the answer unsupported. These are different engineering failures.

According to recent reports, also establish what reviewers should do when the source is outdated. They may correctly conclude that an answer reflects its evidence while separately flagging that evidence as unsuitable for the user's current task.

Start with a calibration batch covering clear successes, unsupported claims, missing evidence, and version mismatches. Have two reviewers label the same items independently, then compare their reasons. Revise ambiguous definitions before increasing volume; the batch is for improving the rubric, not estimating production quality.

Recent findings suggest that keep a rubric version on every review. Labels produced under different definitions should not be mixed without checking comparability.

A spreadsheet can help during exploration, but an engineering pipeline needs a stable record format.

Pydantic can validate a review record before it enters the dataset. Install Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn in your project environment, then use this model:.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError.

model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True).

item_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

answer_revision: str = Field(min_length=1).

snapshot_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

reviewer_id: str = Field(min_length=1).

rubric_version: Literal["auth-v1"].

"supported", "partially_supported",.

completion: Literal["complete", "incomplete", "cannot_assess"].

source_fit: Literal["suitable", "outdated", "cannot_assess"].

rationale: str = Field(min_length=20, max_length=2000).

Strict mode limits type coercion, and extra="forbid" rejects unexpected fields. The model checks shape and allowed values; it cannot establish that a judgment is correct. A minimum rationale length does not guarantee a useful explanation. The snapshot ID references a manifest, which can also record that retrieval produced no usable passages.

Industry observers note that on the server, resolve the item, answer revision, snapshot, and passage IDs against the stored run. Reject IDs that do not belong together. Obtain the reviewer identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a submitted reviewer_id. Store a server-generated submission time and preserve review revisions instead of silently overwriting earlier judgments.

Industry observers note that run this after the model definition. It accepts one fictional review and rejects both an unknown label and an extra field:.

"answer_revision": "answer-02",.

"rationale": "The answer invents X-API-Key; p1 requires Bearer.",.

review = Review.model_validate(payload).

{**payload, "support": "mostly_fine"},.

{**payload, "confidence": 0.99}.

except ValidationError as error:.

print(error.errors()[0]["type"]).

raise AssertionError("Invalid review was accepted").

According to recent reports, the expected error types are literal_error and extra_forbidden. Add separate integration tests for mismatched evidence IDs, unauthorized submissions, and retries. Use a database uniqueness rule or an idempotency key so a repeated request does not create a second independent review.

According to recent reports, more reviews do not automatically produce better evidence. If a task is ambiguous, scaling it can simply reproduce the ambiguity.

The workflow needs clear eligibility requirements, examples, escalation routes, and acceptance criteria. Reviewers assessing API behavior may need domain knowledge that general writing fluency does not provide.

If you work with an external AI-data contributor service such as Acquirox, define the task contract before assigning work: required expertise, permitted source material, output fields, and escalation rules. Keep ownership of the rubric, evaluation set, and acceptance decisions within the product team. Contributor capacity alone does not establish expertise in the API being reviewed.

In a recent development, pilot the actual task in the review interface. Track drafts, submitted reviews, items needing adjudication, and final decisions as distinct workflow states. Reviewer judgments should remain immutable once submitted; corrections should create a new revision with a reason. Keep adjudication separate from the original labels.

According to recent reports, for data involving people or contributors, document permitted uses, access boundaries, and retention. Remove credentials and unnecessary personal information from review material. An internal support transcript should not become a broadly accessible annotation task by accident.

Distinguish annotation from usability research. A skilled reviewer can judge whether an answer is supported, but that does not prove a first-time user can understand the interface.

SitePoint’s guide to choosing usability tests and participants offers related guidance on matching participants and methods to the question being investigated.

The review interface shapes the data it collects.

Label Studio is an option for configurable labeling interfaces and data import/export. If you use it, map exported annotations into the Review schema through an adapter; do not assume its export structure matches your application contract. A custom interface may be appropriate when reviewers need API-version navigation or passage-level citations.

For the documentation assistant, show:.

The original question and relevant user context.

The evidence snapshot supplied to the model.

Separate controls for support and task completion.

A rationale field and an explicit “cannot assess” option.

Display stable passage IDs beside the evidence and let reviewers attach those IDs to their rationale. Show the source version and retrieval time near each passage. Render retrieved content as untrusted text or sanitized markup, and never treat instructions embedded in a source document as reviewer instructions. Avoid loading executable third-party content inside the review panel.

Avoid showing a preferred model name or a previous reviewer's verdict before an independent judgment. For pairwise comparisons, randomize answer order and include appropriate tie or neither-acceptable outcomes.

Design for keyboard use, visible focus, readable text, and explicit selection states. Keep evidence and the answer accessible without requiring excessive horizontal scrolling.

According to recent reports, start all judgment controls unselected and validate them on submission. Use labeled radio groups, an accessible error summary, and visible saving/submission status. A failed save should preserve the draft. Disable duplicate submissions in the UI, but enforce duplicate handling on the server as well.

Practical check: observe a reviewer completing several borderline examples. Record where they pause, misinterpret a label, or cannot find the necessary source material.

When two reviewers disagree, investigate before reducing their decisions to a majority vote.

Different assumptions about the user's expertise.

A genuine error by one or both reviewers.

Sources indicate that preserve independent labels and store the adjudicated result separately. This allows the team to study ambiguity instead of erasing it.

For two reviewers applying categorical labels to the same items, scikit-learn provides Cohen's kappa:.

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score.

("q1", "a1", "s1", "auth-v1"): "supported",.

("q2", "a1", "s2", "auth-v1"): "unsupported",.

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "supported",.

("q4", "a1", "s4", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported".

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported".

raise ValueError("Review sets must contain identical items").

left = [a[key] for key in keys].

right = [b[key] for key in keys].

raw_agreement = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(left, right)) / len(keys).

print(f"Raw agreement: {raw_agreement:.2f}").

print(f"Kappa: {cohen_kappa_score(left, right):.2f}").

This toy example prints raw agreement of 0.75 and kappa of about 0.64. Four items are not enough to assess a review program. In production, check for duplicate reviews before building dictionaries, use one rubric version per comparison, report unmatched items, and align all records by item, answer revision, and evidence snapshot.

Kappa measures agreement beyond chance under its assumptions, not correctness. Inspect raw agreement, label frequencies, and the disagreement table alongside it. A single-category batch can make kappa undefined; report that limitation rather than substituting a reassuring score. Treat cannot_assess explicitly and report its frequency instead of silently excluding difficult cases.

If both reviewers apply the same flawed rubric consistently, agreement can be high while the evaluation remains unhelpful.

According to recent reports, once difficult cases are adjudicated, turn them into regression cases with explicit acceptance criteria. For the fictional authentication task: use version 3 evidence, cite the passage requiring Bearer, and do not invent a header. If version 3 evidence is missing, an acceptable response should explain the gap rather than provide confident instructions.

Source snapshot and document version.

Expected behavior or acceptance criteria.

Model and prompt configuration.

Review and adjudication records.

According to recent reports, DVC can track larger datasets alongside Git. In an existing Git repository with DVC initialized and data/reviewed-auth.jsonl present, a minimal versioning step is:.

dvc add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.

git add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.dvc data/.gitignore.

git commit -m "Version authentication review cases".

Industry observers note that this commits metadata, not the dataset bytes. Configure an access-controlled DVC remote and push the data before expecting another machine or CI runner to retrieve it. Keep credentials and sensitive review material out of public repositories.

In a recent development, keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. If developers repeatedly tune prompts against the same questions, those questions become less useful as evidence of generalization.

Split related examples together where appropriate. Near-duplicate questions from one support conversation should not be scattered across development and evaluation sets.

Use two evaluation passes. First, hold the evidence snapshot fixed to compare answer-generation changes. Then test retrieval against the intended document versions to detect stale or irrelevant sources. Record per-item outcomes and report failures by category; an overall improvement can hide a regression in version-specific or multilingual questions.

SitePoint’s article on testing nondeterministic AI behavior provides further context for repeatable evaluation workflows.

A correct answer can still fail in the interface.

Consumers may overlook a caveat, misunderstand whether an operation has been performed, or miss that the evidence applies to an older API version.

Pair answer review with practical usability tasks:.

Find the authentication requirements for version 3 and identify the source that supports them.

Observe whether customers complete the task and whether their confidence matches the available evidence.

SitePoint’s overview of user research methods helps distinguish task observation from preference surveys.

In a recent development, turn interface failures into browser tests: a citation opens the expected document version, its passage ID matches the displayed evidence, missing evidence offers a recovery action, and a failed review submission preserves the draft. Verify that reviewers cannot access unassigned restricted items by changing an ID in the URL. These checks complement human judgments; they do not replace them.

Recent findings suggest that do not use a fluent response as a substitute for a clear interaction. The interface should distinguish retrieved information, generated interpretation, and actions the application has actually completed.

In a recent development, start with one authentication task, a versioned rubric, and a small calibration batch. Use Pydantic for ingestion checks, Label Studio or a custom interface for review, scikit-learn for agreement analysis, and Git/DVC for dataset provenance. Add each tool only when it solves a concrete workflow need.

At release time, run deterministic checks for schema, evidence references, permissions, and interface behavior. Compare candidate answers against adjudicated acceptance criteria and send upcoming ambiguous failures back for review. Record the dataset revision and configurations with the results so another developer can reproduce the comparison.

The purpose of human review is to produce evidence the team can act on. A smaller collection of well-defined, traceable judgments is often more useful than a large pile of ratings whose meaning nobody can explain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Police departments across the United States are warning GTA 6 players not to recreate crimes from the game in real life, reminding fans that stealing cars and reckless driving have serious consequences outside Vice City.
  • Rockstar Games’ long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 finally rolled out on November 19, bringing players back to Vice City after a 13-year wait between mainline GTA releases.
  • However, with millions of gamers diving into Rockstar’s open world, several American police departments have issued warnings about copying the game’s criminal activities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Police departments across the United States are warning GTA 6 players not to recreate crimes from the game in real life, reminding fans that stealing cars and reckless driving have serious consequences outside Vice City.

Rockstar Games’ long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 finally rolled out on November 19, bringing players back to Vice City after a 13-year wait between mainline GTA releases.

However, with millions of gamers diving into Rockstar’s open world, several American police departments have issued warnings about copying the game’s criminal activities.

In a social media post shared ahead of launch, the Atlanta Police Department warned fans against bringing the chaos into the real world.

“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department wrote. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”.

Recent findings suggest that GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!🎮Don't confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.Drunk driving, reckless driving, auto theft and violence have real consequences.Keep it in the game. Don't bring it to our streets. pic.twitter.com/Y7PdJFHLsZ.

Police specifically highlighted drunk driving, reckless driving, auto theft, and violence, urging players to remember that committing these offenses can have real consequences.

The South Fulton Police Department issued a similar warning, reminding players that fictional crimes have no place on real streets.

Recent findings suggest that “Video games are fiction. Real crimes have real victims, and dangerous driving can change lives forever,” the department said. “There’s no respawn, restart, or undo button.”.

The warnings haven’t been limited to Georgia.

As reported by the San Antonio Express-News, police departments in Texas have also been reminding players to keep their criminal activities confined to the game.

The San Juan Police Department published a GTA-inspired Instagram video featuring an officer closing a jail cell door alongside the franchise’s iconic “Busted” message.

Police can’t wait for GTA 6 to be released so they can “catch a break”.

Newly introduced GTA 6 gameplay is so realistic fans can’t believe it’s not real life.

Police mock man for missing GTA 6 after dangerous car chase leads to arrest.

A post shared by San Juan Police Department (@sjtxpd).

“We know you’re exciting and we know you’ve been waiting a long time, but what happens in GTA VI stays in GTA VI,” they said.

Meanwhile, Floresville police warned that their city wasn’t an extension of Los Santos or Vice City and reminded players that officers aren’t NPCs.

They also warned that running red lights could result in a traffic stop, while changing a car’s color in an H-E-B parking lot wouldn’t make a real-world wanted level disappear.

Interestingly, these warnings come after the Greensboro Police Department in North Carolina mentioned it couldn’t wait for GTA 6 to launch, hoping the game would keep people indoors and give officers a break.

Meanwhile, police in the UK have already used GTA 6 to mock a criminal who was arrested following a dangerous car chase, joking that he would now miss the game’s release.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Despite multiple attempts to remove the hat from her system, Fiona’s condition became a medical emergency, and she ultimately did not recover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fiona, the beloved hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, has died after accidentally swallowing a hat that became lodged in her habitat.

The zoo declared her death on November 19, revealing that its veterinary team had spent days attempting to save her after the incident occurred last week.

Despite multiple attempts to remove the hat from her system, Fiona’s condition became a medical emergency, and she ultimately did not recover.

In a statement shared on Instagram, the Cincinnati Zoo explained that Fiona had accidentally ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat last week.

“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote.

According to the statement, veterinary staff made several attempts to remove the object, but were unable to do so successfully.

“The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome.”.

A post shared by Cincinnati Zoo (@cincinnatizoo).

The zoo confirmed that Fiona received necessary supportive care on November 19 in a final attempt to save her life, but the treatment was unsuccessful.

Fiona became an international sensation after being born prematurely at the Cincinnati Zoo in January 2017. Weighing just 29 pounds at birth, she required round-the-clock care from zoo staff before eventually growing into one of the facility’s most recognizable animals.

Her early development was documented extensively on social media, attracting millions of followers and making her a prominent figure in the zoo’s conservation and educational efforts.

The zoo acknowledged the impact her death would have on the community, writing, “We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are.”.

It also asked visitors and supporters to respect the privacy of the keepers who had cared for Fiona throughout her life.

According to recent reports, “Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time.”.

GTA 6 glitch lets players access first-person mode

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dexerto

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A GTA 6 player has discovered a glitch that lets fans experience Rockstar’s new open-world game in first-person, despite the feature being unavailable at launch.
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 finally rolled out on November 19, but unlike GTA 5, the game doesn’t include a dedicated first-person mode.
  • Rockstar previously explained that development was focused on third-person animations, although players can still use a first-person perspective in certain situations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GTA 6 player has discovered a glitch that lets fans experience Rockstar’s new open-world game in first-person, despite the feature being unavailable at launch.

Grand Theft Auto 6 finally rolled out on November 19, but unlike GTA 5, the game doesn’t include a dedicated first-person mode.

Rockstar previously explained that development was focused on third-person animations, although players can still use a first-person perspective in certain situations.

However, just hours after release, a player discovered a workaround that allows them to explore Vice City through the eyes of Jason and Lucia, complete with weapon animations.

A GTA 6 player discovered a method/glitch to play in first-person mode, which seems to be functional.– Settings → Controller → Touch Pad Button → change to Camera– Sit in the driver’s seat and pull out the phone by pressing ↑ on the d-pad– Put your phone away by pressing… pic.twitter.com/W06K0Bb4Ft.

The discovery was shared to YouTube by ‘oneboyler,’ detailing the find.

On PS5, players need to change their touchpad settings from opening the map to switching cameras. They must then enter a vehicle, open their in-game phone, and rapidly press Circle and the touchpad to trigger the glitch.

If successful, the camera becomes stuck in first-person, allowing players to leave their vehicle and explore the world without returning to the traditional third-person view.

The footage shows the player walking around and using weapons, with animations already appearing to support the perspective.

“As you can see, the weapon animations for first person mode are already in the game,” the uploader explained.

“This is the only way to experience GTA VI in first person mode, since the game for whatever reason didn’t release with it enabled.”.

There is one major drawback, however. Once the glitch is activated, players cannot simply switch back to third-person. Instead, they must reload their save.

The latest discovery suggests that some first-person functionality remains accessible in the finished game, even if Rockstar hasn’t officially enabled it.

Huge GTA 6 leak reveals first-person gameplay despite Rockstar ruling it out at launch.

Rockstar boss explains GTA 6 gun change that will get you in more trouble than before.

How to play first person in GTA Online and best settings.

It’s unclear whether the developers plan to introduce a complete first-person mode in a future patch or patch the glitch to prevent players from accessing it.

For now, it’s another discovery from GTA 6’s launch day, which has already seen fans uncover Dexter Morgan’s apartment and his signature killing tools hidden in Vice City.

Sooner or later someone on your team asks it. Maybe it’s a product manager, maybe the head of content, maybe a teacher who’s just marked forty near-identical essays: can we tell when people are pasting in ChatGPT output?

The short answer is no, not with certainty. Anyone who promises you that is selling something.

Sources indicate that but you can get a useful signal, and you can show it to the people who actually make the call: editors, teachers, moderators. In this tutorial you’ll build a small Express app that takes some text, sends it to an AI detector API, waits for the result, and highlights the sentences that look machine-written.

In a recent development, I’m using the Quetext AI Detector API here. It scores each sentence, not just the whole document, and you can try it without a subscription. Most detection APIs follow the same submit, poll, fetch pattern, though. If you switch providers later, you’ll rewrite one file.

According to recent reports, put the key in an environment variable. Don’t hard-code it, and don’t let it anywhere near the browser.

You’ll make three calls. Analysis takes a few seconds, so the API hands you a ticket and makes you come back for the result. Keep the Quetext API docs open in another tab while you follow along; they list every endpoint, field and error code.

Sources indicate that every request sends your key in an X-API-Key header. The minimum input is 50 words, which sounds annoying until you realise no detector can say anything useful about a two-line comment.

And remember this number: 10 requests every 5 seconds, per account. Progress checks count. It’ll come back to bite you in the production section if you ignore it.

Create quetext.js. I like keeping everything provider-specific in one file, so the rest of the app has no idea who’s doing the detecting.

Three decisions in there that are worth a sentence each:.

The errors keep their HTTP status code. A 402 means you’ve run out of credit and a 429 means you’re polling too fast, and you’ll want to handle those differently from “something broke.”.

Industry observers note that it polls every 2.5 seconds because Quetext’s docs suggest 2 to 3. Polling faster won’t speed the report up. You’ll just burn through the rate limit.

In a recent development, and there’s a hard timeout. Leave it out and one stuck report can hang a request forever. That’s a miserable bug to track down at 11pm.

In a recent development, next, server.js. It checks the input, runs the three calls, and gives the frontend a simple response that doesn’t mention Quetext anywhere.

According to recent reports, look at the mapping at the end. generated_prob becomes probability, and ai_score comes back as a string like "82.50", so it gets parsed into a number. It’s a small detail. But it means your frontend never learns which provider’s field names it’s dealing with, and that’s what makes swapping providers a one-file change.

Show someone “64% AI” and they’ll jump to a conclusion. Show them a paragraph with three sentences shaded pink and they’ll actually read it.

So the page shows every sentence, coloured by how likely it is to be AI-generated. Create public/index.html:.

Run node server.js and open http://localhost:3000. Try two samples: something you wrote yourself, then a raw chatbot answer on the same topic. Seeing which sentences light up teaches you more about how these detectors work than any diagram I could draw.

A quick security point. Those sentences came from your users, then went through an outside service. Treat them as untrusted. That’s why the code uses textContent and never innerHTML, as the OWASP XSS prevention cheat sheet recommends.

The demo keeps an HTTP request open while it polls. Fine on your laptop. Not fine with real traffic.

Submit the text, save the report id with a pending status, and respond straight away. A worker (BullMQ, a cron job, a serverless queue, whatever you already use) does the polling and updates the record once it’s done. The UI says “Checking…” until the result highlights up.

Recent findings suggest that here’s how it goes wrong. It’s Monday morning, 20 editors open their review queues and click “Check” at roughly the same time. Each request polls on its own, and within a few seconds you’ve hit 429s across the board, because the 10-per-5-seconds limit covers your whole account, not each user.

Sources indicate that use one worker that loops through every pending report, with a short pause between calls. Problem solved.

You pay per word, so don’t check every blog comment. Article submissions, assignments and paid freelance work usually justify the cost. Cache results against a hash of the text too. Someone who submits the same draft three times shouldn’t cost you three times.

AI detection doesn’t catch copying. Someone can lift a 2019 blog post word for word and it’ll score 0% AI, because a human wrote it. Just not this human. If originality matters to your product, the same API has plagiarism endpoints that work exactly the same way. The API documentation covers both.

Developers skip this part. It’s also the part that ends up in angry support tickets.

According to recent reports, in 2023, Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran essays written by non-native English speakers (all human, written for the TOEFL) through seven AI detectors. On average, the detectors labelled more than 61% of them as AI-generated. Simple vocabulary and textbook grammar read as “predictable,” and predictability is exactly what detectors look for.

Sources indicate that picture an international student getting an automatic zero because a script remarked so. You don’t want to be the person who built that.

Recent findings suggest that do that and the detector is a fast first pass that points people at what’s worth a closer look. Your humans still make the call.

Industry observers note that you send text, the service checks how predictable each sentence would be to a language model, and you get back a probability that a machine wrote it. Most of these APIs are asynchronous. You submit, get a report ID, poll until it’s ready, then fetch the result. The better ones score individual sentences as well as the whole text, which makes building a sensible review screen much easier.

More than you’d think. Quetext’s API won’t accept fewer than 50 words, and in practice scores settle down once you’re past about 300. A product title or a one-line comment just doesn’t give a detector enough to go on. For short content, either group related pieces together or don’t bother checking it.

No. Detectors make mistakes, and research highlights they flag non-native English writers far more often than native speakers. Use the score to decide what a human looks at first, not to block anything. Give reviewers the highlighted sentences, give users a way to explain themselves, and log what you decided. Your users get treated fairly and your support team avoids a pile of angry tickets.

Poll at the speed the provider recommends (every 2 to 3 seconds for Quetext), and remember that those polls count against your limit too. Once you’re in production, move checks into a background queue and let one worker poll every pending report, rather than having each user request poll by itself. When you do get a 429, wait a moment and retry.

Industry observers note that no. If the browser calls the API directly, your key ends up in the frontend code where anyone can copy it and spend your credit. Keep the key in an environment variable on your server and send requests through your own endpoint, like the one in this tutorial. That also gives you somewhere to check input length, apply per-user limits and cache results before you pay for anything.

GTA 6 players think they’ve found the real-life fursuit that inspired Chase, the fox-suited character you can save from the cops in a viral random encounter.

Sources indicate that being a furry is illegal in GTA 6’s fictional state of Leonida. An in-game TV ad from the Anti-Furry Association urges residents to report suspected furry activity and warns tourists that hunting season is open. Dexerto previously covered the in-game ban and encounter.

The ban plays out in a nighttime standoff, with police surrounding Chase under a helicopter spotlight. Players can give him a ride, lose the cops, and help him and another fursuited character reach the Furverts’ compound.

Despite furries being illegal in GTA 6, you can actually save them if you wantA furry called Chase offers you $15,000 in cash or a custom SMG in exchange for helping them pic.twitter.com/SkZ21atE5r.

Fans comparing Chase with fursuiter FoxiFelix zeroed in on the knees. Both suits have white shooting stars in roughly the same spot on each leg, with three stripes trailing from each star. The fox heads differ, and Felix spotted another resemblance after watching the encounter on YouTube, saying the tails looked alike.

Felix also remarked Chase meowing in the van reminded them of something they do themselves.

I've just watched the encounter on YouTube and holy fuck so much is the same it's wild haha. Even the tail is the heccin same ❤️ The fact that chase starts meowing in the van fucking sent me as THATS LITERALLY WHAT I DO 😅.

Recent findings suggest that YCHsuits, one of the makers Felix credits for their suit, also weighed in. The maker said Rockstar used one of its designs for the furry storyline and added that someone else made the fursuit’s head.

I already did – the basis is off of a suit I made back in 2020 x3 (barring the head).

Another fursuiter, Chase the Fox, stated their DMs blew up after people connected them to the character. The two share a name and wear fox suits, while the shooting-star markings are the detail fans keep pointing to in the FoxiFelix comparison.

My DMs are exploding right now because apparently I'M the furry in GTA VI and I was honestly not prepared to hear that when I woke up today 😭 pic.twitter.com/nTl3KkPvwq.

Rockstar has yet to publicly confirm what inspired Chase’s design.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some GTA 6 players have already found a new favorite in Vicki, a goth bartender they meet just one chapter after Mandy.

Recent findings suggest that vicki works at Delights, a strip club in Port Gellhorn, and lives in Room 10 at the Starlet Motel. Lucia first meets her there in “Girls’ Trip” while looking for painkillers for Jason. When the pills Vicki sells her turn out to be over-the-counter medicine, the two head into town to track down Vicki’s dealer.

It took just one scene in Chapter 1 for Mandy to win over players. She talks Jason into fixing her sink while he’s out collecting money for Brian. The object he pulls from the pipe looks like a severed finger, which led to the theory that Mandy might be a serial killer.

When X user @AerisTreat posted about Vicki on November 20, players in the replies started picking sides.

Oooh shit PT.2 pic.twitter.com/JroGxh3CS2.

Recent findings suggest that “Mandy is so overrated, Vicki is where it’s at,” one player wrote. Another called GTA 6 “Game of the year just for her,” while a third wished the game had a friendship mechanic for side characters so Vicki and Lucia could be best friends.

According to recent reports, one player mentioned they’d already been to Delights and hadn’t seen Vicki behind the bar. AerisTreat told them to look for her on the second story visit to the club, during “Afternoon Delight.”.

Recent findings suggest that the mission opens up after “Coffee Break” in Chapter 2, when Vicki calls Jason and Lucia with a plan to rob her boss, Frankie. It’s ladies’ night when they arrive, and if players agree to help when Frankie asks whether Jason can dance, Jason takes the stage while Lucia goes after the safe.

This one checks Pin and Juicebox against their current public pages.

Sources indicate that pin (pin.com) is an AI recruiting platform that automates the top of the funnel, from sourcing and outreach to interview scheduling, for solo recruiters, agencies and in-house teams. Juicebox (PeopleGPT) is an AI sourcing platform that pairs natural-language candidate search with outreach sequences, ATS and CRM integrations, and add-on AI agents. Sources indicate that no. Pin has a one-seat Solo plan at $99 a month on annual billing, and solo recruiters and small agencies use it. But Pin's team features and pricing are built for multiple users:.

Juicebox does team work too. According to its pricing page (October 2026), Growth lets you invite up to five teammates to collaborate on searches, shortlists and outreach, and Business adds hiring-manager seats, usage analytics and ATS or CRM integration. Pin's team pages describe hiring managers, sourcers and closers sharing one view of the req.

Pin states it searches 850M+ profiles across multiple sources, including North America and Europe, aggregated from professional networks, GitHub, Stack Overflow, open-source contributions, patents, academic publications and the broader web. You can search in plain language, paste a job description, upload ideal résumés or import a role from your ATS. Each ranked candidate gets a fit score and an AI-written reason, and the model learns from accept and reject feedback across the team.

Juicebox offers natural-language search over a stated 800 million profiles from "30+" sources, and its AI Spotlight also explains why a candidate matches. It adds three data features worth knowing about:.

Pin lists Talent Insights on Professional and Business too. Profile counts say little about quality, so run the same roles in both. If you are also pricing LinkedIn's tool, see LinkedIn Recruiter alternatives.

According to recent reports, pin runs multi-channel sequences across email, LinkedIn and SMS: automated email steps plus AI-drafted LinkedIn and SMS tasks in the same sequence, which the recruiter sends. Pin reports those sequences deliver 5x better response rates than industry averages, benchmarked against LinkedIn's published 10-25% InMail reply rates. Pin drafts each message from the candidate's own profile signals and calibrates to your writing voice. Sequences adapt per candidate, any reply pauses the sequence, and every channel stays in one thread. The Free strategy is email-only, multi-channel sequences start on Solo, and Professional includes five mailboxes per user.

Juicebox's outreach page (October 2026) describes "email, calls, and social touches in one sequence," automatic stop on reply and analytics by step and channel. Growth includes three mailboxes per seat, Business six. Its agents page describes agent outreach as email only.

Industry observers note that no. Pin's AI recruiting agent has two modes. In Assist, you approve each step. In Autopilot, the agent sources, screens and ranks, drafts outreach, sends the email steps, follows up on silence, schedules interviews and updates the ATS. LinkedIn and SMS steps queue as tasks with AI-drafted messages that the recruiter sends. Pin assists recruiters and never replaces them: closing and offers stay human. Human-in-the-loop guardrails apply, and every action appears in a feed. Pin saves recruiters 12 hours per week on sourcing and outreach combined, according to Pin's 2026 user survey across 2,000+ organizations and 20,000+ users.

It is also steerable. Pin asks clarifying questions about the brief, such as "Is remote considered?", and you refine in plain language. Josh Volinsky, Co-Founder of Synergy Search, states: "Pin makes sourcing candidates so natural and I love how you can just talk to it like it's a recruiter on your team and it goes hunting.".

Pin's MCP server lets you work from Claude Desktop, Claude Code, ChatGPT or Codex: start searches, review candidates, tune the search in plain language and keep per-job memory. Pin notes "You still approve every accept, reject, and outreach." It is free on every paid plan.

According to its agents page (October 2026), you recalibrate by chatting with the agent, with autonomy from fully hands-off to manual checkpoints at shortlist or sequencing. Its MCP server, rolled out in August 2026, rolls out agents and pulls usage and reply-rate reports. The agents page does not describe interview scheduling, and each agent is a separate $199 monthly add-on.

Pin uses third-party fairness audits and feeds no names, gender or protected characteristics to the AI, with checkpoints at every step and regular team reviews of AI outputs. Its trust center lists a Pin Algorithmic Fairness Report (August 2026), available on request.

It indicated monthly audits of Juicebox's Autopilot candidate-ranking feature, the latest dated August 6, 2026, with reports for NYC Local Law 144, the EU AI Act, Colorado and California.

For recruiting teams and agencies that want one product from sourcing through scheduling, Pin covers that whole flow.

Juicebox is good for: - Teams that need hiring-manager seats to review shortlists, on its custom-priced Business proposal. - Teams that value compensation estimates (Growth and up) or warm-intro network sourcing (Business only).

When Pin is not the right fit: teams that only need high-volume inbound applicant screening.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fortnite’s PlayStation Cup is back in November, giving PlayStation players a chance to compete for a share of $100,000 in cash prizes.
  • According to recent reports, the cup qualifiers start on November 23, with separate competitions for Battle Royale and Zero Build.
  • Here’s how to enter the Fortnite PlayStation Cup on your PlayStation, when each round takes place, and what you can win.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fortnite’s PlayStation Cup is back in November, giving PlayStation players a chance to compete for a share of $100,000 in cash prizes.

According to recent reports, the cup qualifiers start on November 23, with separate competitions for Battle Royale and Zero Build. Both are Solo events, so you can jump in without having to find a duo partner or put a squad together.

Here’s how to enter the Fortnite PlayStation Cup on your PlayStation, when each round takes place, and what you can win.

According to recent reports, before the Cup starts, make sure your PlayStation and Epic Games accounts are linked and that you’ve enabled two-factor authentication. Your Epic account needs to be in good standing and at least level 50, which you can check in the Career tab. You’ll also need to be at least 13 and meet the eligibility requirements for your country.

The Cup starts on Monday, November 23, with qualifiers for both Battle Royale and Zero Build. Top 80 players who advance in Zero Build will compete in the finals on Tuesday, November 24, while the Battle Royale finals take place on Wednesday, November 25.

This gives you just one day to book a spot in the finals, so you’ll have to rack up those wins as quickly as possible.

Industry observers note that each mode has $50,000 in prize money split across seven regions. In Europe, the top 50 finishers in each final earn cash, with $4,000 going to first place. North America Central also pays out to the top 50, with $2,500 for the winner.

In North America West, Brazil, the Middle East, Oceania, and Asia, the top 25 players in each final earn a cash prize, with $750 for first place.

Industry News: Introducing three weeks of specialist GTA - and not-GTA! - programming on Eurogamer

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This idea started as a single theme week, which we thought we might run in the lead up to Grand Theft Auto 6's launch.
  • So, allow me to introduce a whopping three-and-a-bit-ish weeks of specialist GTA- and not-GTA-themed coverage on Eurogamer!
  • It has been revealed that with GTA 6 launching next Thursday, we'll start with a week of coverage dedicated to the series, beginning today with a reader competition (more on that shortly!) and running until next weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hello! This idea started as a single theme week, which we thought we might run in the lead up to Grand Theft Auto 6's launch. Then it turned into a pair of theme weeks. Then we realised we had so much stuff - and that, frankly, GTA 6 would be so dominating it'll be around for far more than a week itself - that we couldn't really fit it into two weeks either.

So, allow me to introduce a whopping three-and-a-bit-ish weeks of specialist GTA- and not-GTA-themed coverage on Eurogamer! (Insert celebratory car horn toots here.).

It has been revealed that with GTA 6 launching next Thursday, we'll start with a week of coverage dedicated to the series, beginning today with a reader competition (more on that shortly!) and running until next weekend. We'll be covering GTA from all angles here - retrospectives, features, launch day coverage and beyond - across the series as a whole, as well as the massive one we've got coming up. You can see that in one place at our GTA Week hub, which will populate as stories go live.

However! If that - coupled with the inevitable wave of coverage that already comes from an enormous moment in video games like this - sounds like the last thing you want from us, well frankly, we get it. Matching massive games with big coverage is a part of the brief at a site like Eurogamer, but it's also far from the only thing we want to be about. And we know it's far from the only thing you're going to want to read about for the rest of November, either.

To counteract that, then: we're also running a solid two weeks of counterprogramming, beginning on Monday 23rd November after GTA 6's launch. Expect all things not-GTA: coverage of lesser-known games, smaller-budget efforts, in-depth features on games and stories that are thematically opposed to it, have nothing to do with it, or take it for inspiration but go in an entirely different direction. All of our special counterprogramming can be found at our Not-GTA hub here as it goes live.

According to recent reports, those of you who've been coming back to Eurogamer for a few years might remember our "Games That Got Away" theme week from a few years back - we're bringing that back in a modified form here, too. Look forward to dedicated write ups - some labelled as reviews, some as broader reflective essays and criticism - on some of the great games we haven't quite found the time for so far this year, as we look to clear our own pile of shame.

Amongst all this, rest assured that normal service is also continuing here as ever. All the essential reporting, criticism, guides and the rest - across all things video games, whether or not that includes the Massive One - will carry on as usual.

Ultimately, our hope is to offer something for everyone with this period - both the people who look to us to be comprehensive across gaming's biggest moments, and those who see us as a place for deep, nuanced, or simply fun stories on the medium's lesser-known corners.

Recent findings suggest that thank you as ever for reading - we really do appreciate it. And on that note, here's a link to Bertie's blog on our readers' competition, where you can win yourself your very own copy of GTA 6.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This piece is part of our GTA Week coverage here on Eurogamer, as we explore all things Grand Theft Auto across the launch period of the wildly anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • UPGRADE 17TH NOVEMBER: Firstly, a big thank you - THANK YOU - because your stories have been delightful to read.
  • You had many similar tales, of friends playing together, siblings playing together, families playing together; heartwarming recollections of days when life seemed simpler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hello! This piece is part of our GTA Week coverage here on Eurogamer, as we explore all things Grand Theft Auto across the launch period of the wildly anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6. For more like this, see our GTA Week hub - or for the exact opposite, look out for our Not-GTA week of counterprogramming, running from 23rd November.

UPGRADE 17TH NOVEMBER: Firstly, a big thank you - THANK YOU - because your stories have been delightful to read. I've laughed and been touched by the power video games have to shape and compliment our lives, and to bring people together. You even inadvertently compelled me to send a message to the old friend I played Vice City and San Andreas with, to tell him what fond memories I have of it. "It was very intense," he replied.

You had many similar tales, of friends playing together, siblings playing together, families playing together; heartwarming recollections of days when life seemed simpler. You also reminded me how games can fill holes in our lives and provide us with escapism when we need it most. And how many of you played the games underage! Some of you were scandalously young. But therein was planted a love for a series that remains to this day.

Industry observers note that the winning entry that I've chosen has continued to make me laugh since I read it. I enjoyed it so much I shared it with the rest of the Eurogamer team and my partner, who also laughed, which is a good sign. For me, this story not only gets at exactly what GTA is as a gaming experience, but also at the power games have to create bonds between people, and the quote the story culminates in is an all-timer: "I'm wanted for murder, Barry. Put the kettle on." Bradley Reiman, congratulations! I'll also pin the comment to make it easy to find.

ORIGINAL STORY 13TH NOVEMBER:These are my favourite competitions to run on Eurogamer, so I'm glad to be able to announce a upcoming one. We'd like you to share your favourite gaming memory related to playing a Grand Theft Auto game - any Grand Theft Auto game - in the comments below, and if we end up liking yours the most, we'll give you a copy of GTA 6.

According to recent reports, I love these competitions because they result in hundreds of funny, heartwarming and often poignant stories about playing games. We've done similar memory-offs for other major gaming franchises in the past: Street Fighter, The Legend of Zelda, Star Wars. We did one about Christmas. We even did one about Eurogamer for our 25th birthday. So it's only right that we do one for arguably the biggest franchise in video games: Grand Theft Auto.

I'll let this run over the weekend and put a deadline of Monday, 16th November at noon UK time on entries. I'll comb through replies early next week in the interest of selecting a winner and giving them - you? - a copy of the game before (or as) GTA 6 releases next Thursday. I notify people using the email address associated with their Eurogamer commenting account, and reply in the comments as well, making it explicitly clear if you've won. Please keep an eye on this thread and your inbox because if I don't hear back, I'll offer the prize elsewhere.

Sources indicate that with that remarked, let's talk memories! I have a couple when it comes to Grand Theft Auto. My earliest memory is of a teenage me playing the first GTA at a friend's house. In a convoluted 90s way, one friend had taken their PC to another friend's house, where the three of us had assembled to play it. We'd take it in turns to burn around the top-down city, and when we weren't at the controls, we'd still be active in the experience, with the huge paper map unfolded, looking for spray shops the player could nip into when chased by the police. It was like being the passenger in a car. I can picture now, almost 30 years later, vividly.

The other distinct GTA memory I have is of playing Vice City and San Andreas one summer after I'd broken my arm and leg. I jumped off a roof in Australia when I was drunk; I wouldn't recommend it. Anyway, upon returning home, there wasn't a lot I could do - the breaks were both on one side so I'd crutch around (they gave me a wooden crutch in Australia) like a pirate - so a friend and I spent that summer taking turns playing GTA. It's all those shared moments laughing at Tommy Vercetti driving up staircases on vintage scooters that I remember, or CJ flapping his wooden-block hands around like paddles while gesticulating in cutscenes. Us just messing around. Friendship. That's what remembering Vice City and San Andreas conjures for me.

But what about you - what do you remember about playing GTA games? Let your mind wander, let your mind remember, and thank you in advance for sharing your stories with us and everyone else. Have a lovely weekend.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Another week has climaxed and I'm so sorry you had to read that on a Saturday morning.
  • According to recent reports, but enough about us, what about you?
  • My favourite thing so far about Ocarina of Time is the judgement plastered on little Link's face when he encounters, well, almost everyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Another week has climaxed and I'm so sorry you had to read that on a Saturday morning. But here we are again, with our regular feature, where we talk about what we've been playing in order that you do too. This week, Marie has been staring at monster butts; Connor has capitulated to World of Warcraft; Kelsey is discovering the joys of a beloved Zelda game for the first time; and Bertie enjoys someone being punched in the face, because I guess he's that sort of person?

According to recent reports, but enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago. And now onward!

My favourite thing so far about Ocarina of Time is the judgement plastered on little Link's face when he encounters, well, almost everyone. Whether he means to or not, he serves sass all over town, and in Kakariko Village, and I am very much here for it.

Industry observers note that also, I wasn't prepared to come face-to-face with a monster's butt cheeks. At all. Imagine the scene: I'm enjoying the tunes of the Lost Woods, processing the changes that have happened to Hyrule in the last seven years, all while making my way to the Forest Temple. Then the Moblin's turn their backs to reveal... Well, everything.

Sources indicate that this week I've spent an ungodly amount of time playing World of Warcraft: Forever (you may have read my preview on the website) and have been essentially glued to it during every minute of free time I've had away from work. I've got both my main professions above the level 225 mark and I'm firmly in the thick of it now. Levels take longer, items are actually getting good, and I've had to make a second alt character for extra bank space.

As a result, I've not been to the gym in a while. I actually got one of those emails asking why I've fallen off, offering some tips to get back into the routine. Sorry Nuffield Health, my sleep schedule is ruined and I've substituted proper workouts for squats and basic at-home cardio. Surely, this can't go wrong...

I don't have the same level of nostalgia for Ocarina of Time that my peers do, but that has not stopped me from enjoying every minute of running around Hyrule smashing pots and trying not to cry over the touching cutscenes and, well, Saria.

According to recent reports, the game feels like Dark Souls for children (endearing) and that is completely my jam. It's magical, satisfying, and often sad. There's creepy enemies as well as cute ones, trap floors and doors, mysterious NPCs... and my heart just feels so warm whenever I'm playing it. My fingers are now crossed that there's a Majora's Mask remake in the pipeline over at Nintendo. (As well as a Super Mario 64 remake, which I admit, is pushing it. But for what it’s worth, I'd probably sell my soul to see it get the Ocarina treatment.).

It takes me a while to settle with games; it takes me a while to settle full stop. I suppose in Fire Emblem's case I'm out of touch, seeing as the last instalment I played was on 3DS. But I struggled with the garish enthusiasm early on and the whole thing seemed overly simple. Nevertheless, I've settled a bit now, and now that the game's layering on more strategy and Intelligent System's expertise is coming to the fore, I'm beginning to enjoy myself much more.

I wasn't expecting it to be quite so boobsy, though. Was Fire Emblem always this way? Perhaps it's my fault for picking the scantily clad queen Theodora, though that sort of presentation isn't reserved only for her. She's no wallflower, though. My favourite moment so far was when she got off her elephant during a parade - yes, her elephant - and walked over to punch a teenage boy in the face for halting proceedings. Apparently she was doing him a favour.
